lesson.title: The Secret Switch: Why if __name__ == "__main__": Exists
lesson.summary: Every Python file carries a hidden variable, __name__, that tells it whether it is being run directly or imported by another file, and that distinction lets one file act as both a reusable module and a standalone script.
lesson.body:
You already know two separate ideas that this concept quietly merges. First, the main function pattern: wrapping a script's top-level actions in a function, often called main(), instead of letting them run loose at the top of the file. Second, Python modules: any .py file can be imported by another file to reuse its functions and classes, the same way you would import math or random. The question this concept answers is: what happens when a single file needs to do both jobs, sometimes it is run directly as a script, and sometimes it is imported so another file can borrow its functions?

Python solves this with a built-in variable that every module automatically has: __name__. When you run a file directly, for example by typing python temperature.py at the command line, Python sets that file's __name__ to the string "__main__". But when that same file is imported from somewhere else, Python sets __name__ to the module's own name instead, the filename without the .py ending. Nothing about the file's code changes between these two situations. Only the value of __name__ changes, and your code can check it.

That check is the pattern if __name__ == "__main__":. Any code placed inside that block only runs when the file is executed directly, never when it is imported. This matters because importing a file should not have unwanted side effects. If you write a module full of useful functions but also sprinkle print statements and test calls directly at the top level, every single one of those runs the instant someone else imports your file, even though all they wanted was to borrow one function. The guard lets you keep the demonstration or entry-point code in the file, right next to the functions it demonstrates, without that code leaking out whenever the file is reused as a module.

Here is a single file that behaves differently depending on how it is started.

```python
# temperature.py
def celsius_to_fahrenheit(c):
    return c * 9 / 5 + 32

print("temperature.py's __name__ is:", __name__)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(celsius_to_fahrenheit(100))
```

Run this file directly with python temperature.py and both lines execute, because __name__ equals "__main__" here:

```
temperature.py's __name__ is: __main__
212.0
```

But suppose a different file does import temperature at the top. Now __name__ inside temperature.py is set to "temperature" instead, so the guarded block is skipped entirely, only the unguarded print statement runs during the import:

```
temperature.py's __name__ is: temperature
```

and the other file can freely call temperature.celsius_to_fahrenheit(0) whenever it wants, without triggering the print(212.0) line that was meant only for standalone runs. This one small if statement is what lets professional Python files serve double duty: a library when imported, a runnable program when executed on its own.
